title: Asymmetric (Public-Key) Cryptography
summary: Public/private key pairs, RSA and elliptic curve cryptography at a conceptual level, and why real systems like TLS use asymmetric crypto only to exchange a symmetric key rather than to encrypt data directly.

slides.markdown:
Symmetric encryption has one unsolved problem baked in: both parties need the *same* secret key before they can communicate, and safely getting that key to both sides over a public network is exactly as hard as the problem encryption was supposed to solve. **Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography** breaks that circularity with a key *pair* — one half can be shared with the entire internet, the other half never leaves its owner.

This topic covers the mental model behind key pairs, RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) as the two dominant families, why asymmetric math is inherently slow, and the pattern — hybrid encryption — that every real system uses to get both asymmetric's key-distribution win and symmetric's speed at the same time.

slides.subTitle: The mental model, made rigorous
slides.markdown:
Every asymmetric scheme starts from a **mathematically related pair of keys**: a **public key**, which can be published anywhere — a website, a key server, an email signature — and a **private key**, which must never leave its owner's control.

The rigor that makes this useful, not just a naming convention: the pair is generated together from an underlying hard mathematical problem, such that operations with one key can only be efficiently undone with the *other* key in the pair — not with a copy of the same key, and not by deriving one key from the other in reasonable time. Encrypt with the public key, and only the matching private key can decrypt. Sign with the private key, and anyone with the public key can verify — but not forge a new valid signature.

This single property is what solves the problem symmetric encryption can't: a stranger with no prior relationship to you can grab your public key and send you something only you can read, with no shared secret ever having existed between you. That capability — communicating securely with someone you've never met — is the entire reason this branch of cryptography exists.

slides.subTitle: A trapdoor function built on factoring
slides.markdown:
RSA's security rests on a **trapdoor function**: an operation that's easy to compute in one direction and, without a specific secret, computationally infeasible to reverse — but *is* easy to reverse if you hold that secret.

Concretely, and conceptually rather than with the actual number theory: RSA generates a public/private key pair from two large prime numbers. Multiplying those primes together to get their product is trivially fast — this product is part of the public key. Going the other direction — **factoring** that large product back into its original two primes — is believed to be computationally infeasible for sufficiently large numbers (RSA keys today are typically 2048 or 4096 bits) with any known classical algorithm. The private key is derived from those original primes, so only whoever generated the key pair can efficiently do the operations that require them.

This is why RSA key sizes look so large compared to AES: RSA's security doesn't come from exhausting a key space by brute force, it comes from factoring being hard, and factoring gets *easier relative to key size* as numbers grow, unlike a symmetric key space, which is why RSA needs thousands of bits to match what AES achieves in a few hundred.

slides.subTitle: Same guarantee, much smaller keys
slides.markdown:
**Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC)** provides the same public/private key-pair guarantee as RSA, built on a different hard problem: the difficulty of reversing a specific operation (point multiplication) on the mathematical structure of an elliptic curve, rather than the difficulty of factoring.

The practical payoff is key size: a **256-bit ECC key** offers security roughly comparable to a **3072-bit RSA key**, because the best known attacks against elliptic curves are far less effective per bit than the best known attacks against factoring. Smaller keys mean faster key generation, smaller certificates and signatures, and less computation per operation — which is why ECC has become the default for new systems where RSA was once standard: modern TLS certificates increasingly use ECDSA (ECC-based signatures) instead of RSA signatures, and mobile and IoT devices favor ECC specifically because the smaller keys and faster operations matter more on constrained hardware.

ECC isn't a strictly "better" replacement in every dimension — RSA's math is simpler to implement correctly, which has historically mattered for security-critical code — but for new systems without a specific legacy constraint, ECC's efficiency advantage at equivalent security is usually the deciding factor.

slides.sectionTitle: Why asymmetric operations are computationally expensive
slides.markdown:
Symmetric encryption (AES) and asymmetric encryption (RSA, ECC) are not just different math — they're different *orders of magnitude* of computational cost, and the reason is structural, not an implementation detail waiting to be optimized away.

AES's rounds are simple bitwise and byte-level operations — substitutions and permutations — that map efficiently onto both CPU instructions and dedicated hardware (most modern CPUs have AES instructions built in). RSA and ECC operations involve modular exponentiation over very large numbers (RSA) or repeated point arithmetic on a curve (ECC) — mathematically necessary for the trapdoor property to hold, but inherently far more expensive per operation, often by two to three orders of magnitude for equivalent-sized data.

This isn't a gap that better engineering closes — it's fundamental to why the trapdoor works at all: an operation that's *cheap* to reverse without the secret would defeat the entire security model. The expense is the price paid for the specific mathematical property that makes public-key cryptography useful in the first place, which is exactly why no real system uses asymmetric crypto to encrypt bulk data directly.

slides.subTitle: Asymmetric crypto only to exchange a key
slides.markdown:
**Hybrid encryption** is the pattern every real-world system actually uses: use asymmetric cryptography only for the small, one-time job of exchanging a symmetric key, then switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual bulk data.

The sequence: the sender generates a random symmetric key (a fresh AES key, used just for this session or message), encrypts *that key* — a tiny amount of data — with the recipient's public key, and sends both the encrypted key and the AES-encrypted payload together. The recipient decrypts the small encrypted key with their private key (the one expensive asymmetric operation, done once, on a small input), then uses that recovered symmetric key to decrypt the actual payload at AES speed.

This gets the best of both worlds without compromise: asymmetric crypto's solved key-distribution problem (no pre-shared secret needed) plus symmetric crypto's speed for the data that actually matters in volume. Every protocol you've used that mixes "public key" and "fast encrypted data" — TLS, PGP/GPG email, most VPN protocols — is running exactly this pattern under a different name.

slides.subTitle: This is how TLS and PGP actually work
slides.markdown:
![Hybrid encryption flow: the AES session key is encrypted once with the recipient's public key while the bulk payload is encrypted continuously with fast symmetric AES, then both travel together to the recipient](assets/hybrid-encryption-flow.svg)

The labels on the diagram are the point: the expensive asymmetric operation happens exactly once, on a few hundred bytes, no matter how large the actual message or session turns out to be. Everything that scales with data volume — an entire TLS session's worth of web traffic, an entire encrypted email attachment — runs through the cheap symmetric path. This is why hybrid encryption has essentially zero performance downside compared to pure symmetric encryption, while still solving the key-distribution problem pure symmetric encryption can't.

slides.subTitle: Key size, performance, adoption
slides.markdown:
| | RSA | ECC |
|---|---|---|
| **Hard problem** | Factoring large numbers | Elliptic curve discrete logarithm |
| **Key size for ~128-bit security** | ~3072 bits | ~256 bits |
| **Relative speed** | Slower at equivalent security, especially key generation | Faster, smaller keys, less computation per operation |
| **Implementation complexity** | Simpler math, well-understood pitfalls | More subtle to implement correctly (curve choice, point validation) |
| **Typical use today** | Legacy systems, some certificate chains, environments requiring RSA compatibility | Default choice for new systems, mobile/IoT, modern TLS certificates (ECDSA) |

The historical trend across the industry has been a steady migration from RSA toward ECC for new deployments, driven almost entirely by the size and speed advantage — smaller keys mean smaller certificates to transmit, faster handshakes, and less battery drain on constrained devices. RSA hasn't disappeared because of compatibility requirements with older systems and existing certificate infrastructure, not because it's been broken.

slides.sectionTitle: Encrypting a large payload directly with RSA
slides.markdown:
A recurring mistake from engineers who understand RSA conceptually but haven't internalized why hybrid encryption exists: encrypting an entire file, message body, or API payload directly with someone's RSA public key, instead of using RSA only to wrap a symmetric key.

This fails for two separate, compounding reasons. First, **performance**: RSA is orders of magnitude slower than AES for the same amount of data — direct RSA encryption of anything beyond a tiny payload is often impractically slow. Second, and more fundamentally, **RSA has a strict maximum message size** tied to its key length (roughly the key size in bytes, minus padding overhead) — a 2048-bit RSA key can encrypt at most a few hundred bytes in one operation. There's no way to directly RSA-encrypt a multi-megabyte file at all; the operation simply doesn't support it, padding scheme details aside.

The fix is always hybrid encryption: generate a random AES key, encrypt the actual payload with AES, and use RSA only to encrypt that small AES key. This isn't a workaround or an optimization — it's the only correct pattern, and any library or tutorial suggesting direct RSA encryption of substantial data is demonstrating exactly the mistake this slide is naming.

This topic has focused on asymmetric crypto's *encryption* use — solving key distribution via hybrid encryption. The same public/private key-pair mechanism has a second, equally important use that the next topic covers in full: **signing**. Sign with the private key, verify with the public key, and you get proof of authorship and tamper-detection combined — non-repudiation, which HMAC's shared-key construction can't provide, because with HMAC either party could have produced the tag.

Digital Signatures & PKI picks up exactly there: how signatures work mechanically (hash the message, sign the hash — tying back to [Hashing & Message Integrity](hashing-integrity)), and how certificates and certificate authorities let a public key be trustworthily tied to a real-world identity, not just mathematically valid.

The throughline worth holding onto: asymmetric crypto's entire value, in both encryption and signing, comes from the same one property — an operation with one key that only the matching key in the pair can undo — applied to two different problems.
